newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Yemen said to play key role in illegal rhino trade.
newsitem.headline: Yemen said to play key role in illegal rhino trade.

text.p: Yemen plays a central role in illicit trade in African rhinoceros horn, worsening the endangered species' perilous status on the continent, a wildlife trade monitoring programme (TRAFFIC) said in a report on Wednesday.

TRAFFIC estimated at least 75 kilos (165 pounds) of rhino horn had been smuggled into Yemen every year between 1994 and 1996. "This amount could originate from up to 25 rhinoceroses," it said in a statement.

Rhino horn is prized in Yemen for use in the handles of traditional daggers known as jambiyas, according to TRAFFIC. Its investigators saw craftsmen filing new handles in late 1996 while traders alleged that illegal imports continued, mainly from Eastern Africa.
TRAFFIC called on Yemen to strengthen its national laws banning imports and to combat illegal trade in rhino horn, including promotion of substitute materials for dagger handles.
"For 15 years, Yemen has been under international pressure to halt this persistent drain on rhinoceros populations in Africa," said TRAFFIC executive director Stephen Broad.
"Some important steps have been taken by the Yemen government, but our latest investigations show that significant smuggling continues and simply not enough is being done to bring it to a halt."
TRAFFIC is the wildlife trade monitoring programme of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) and the World Conservation Union (IUCN), both based in Gland, Switzerland.
Yemen has not joined CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, according to the statement issued by the two agencies.
"Yemen should join CITES, an action it has been promising since at least 1992," it added.

International commercial trade in rhinoceroses and their products has been banned under CITES since 1977, but member countries will meet next month to examine the parlous state of rhineroceros species and problems of continued illegal trade.
Thre are fewer than 10,000 rhinos remaining in the wild in Africa, compared to 70,000 in 1970, TRAFFIC said.

"Snared, speared, shot with poisoned arrows and bullets for their horns, rhino numbers in most populations have plummeted," it said. "The demand and trade in horn for jambiyas has been a major contributor."
